title: Free a panel from a leaning rack, moving only what leans on it
instruction: Stand the red panel upright on the white inspection plate, and stand any panel you move upright on the black mat.
context: Sheet goods such as glass, stone slabs, solar modules and honeycomb sandwich panels are stored on edge in racks, leaning on each other. Pulling a sheet that others lean on drops them, a known crush hazard in glass and stone yards, and every sheet handled is another chance to break one, so a rigger moves only the sheets that bear on the one needed, in dependency order. Spacecraft structure panels on rack carts in an integration hall pose the same question. Here two blue panels lean on the red target in a chain, while the grey panel beside it stands on its own. The instruction names neither the order nor which panels to move; the rails show it: a panel centred on a wide rail stands alone, one whose narrow rail lies wholly outside its centre leans inward. Physics, not a stated rule, punishes the wrong order. Unlike unloading one balanced plank, the policy must work out which loose panels depend on the target and leave the rest alone. 1 g tabletop analogue; no microgravity is claimed.
setup: Table coordinates in metres: x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y left from the midline, z up from the table top; the left arm's base is at y = 0.305, the right arm's at y = -0.305. All the work is in front of the left arm, within 0.30 m of its base; the right arm stays at its ready pose. Fixed, light grey (sRGB 0.75, 0.76, 0.78) anodised aluminium: a rack of four rails, each 90 mm long along x (x 0.215 to 0.305) and 20 mm tall, standing on the table and spanning y 0.1575 to 0.2015 (grey rail, 44 mm), 0.2160 to 0.2640 (red rail, 48 mm), 0.3105 to 0.3245 (inner blue rail, 14 mm) and 0.3710 to 0.3910 (outer blue rail, 20 mm), with open slots to the table between them, 14.5, 46.5 and 46.5 mm wide. Fixed: a black (sRGB 0.12, 0.12, 0.13) rubber mat 80 x 240 x 2 mm centred at (0.160, 0.470); a white (sRGB 0.92, 0.92, 0.90) acetal inspection plate 100 x 100 x 3 mm centred at (0.170, 0.080). Loose, rigid, matte: four panels, blocks 50 mm deep along x, 60 mm wide along y and 100 mm tall, standing on the rails (bottoms 20 mm up) centred at x = 0.270, 0.5 mm apart at the foot: grey (sRGB 0.55, 0.57, 0.60), 70 g, centred at y = 0.1795; red (sRGB 0.80, 0.15, 0.12), 140 g, at y = 0.2400; inner blue (sRGB 0.20, 0.40, 0.80), 70 g, at y = 0.3005; outer blue, same colour, 70 g, at y = 0.3610. The grey and red panels stand centred on their rails and stand on their own. Each blue panel stands on a rail under only the outer third of its foot, its centre of mass 10 mm past the rail's inner edge, over a slot, so the inner blue panel leans on the red panel and the outer blue panel leans on the inner blue one. The outer blue panel presses on the inner blue one with about 0.07 N at the top; the inner blue panel presses on the red one with about 0.14 N, its own lean plus the outer panel's. The red panel's rail resists that 2.4 times over, with or without the grey panel beside it. In simulation the panels spawn upright and, in the 0.5 s settle before the trial, the inner blue panel tips 0.3 degrees and the outer blue panel 0.6 degrees onto their neighbours, as the 0.5 mm gaps over the 100 mm height allow. A panel on the flat mat or plate stands alone. To build it: cut the rails from 20 mm aluminium flat bar (or print them in PLA) and screw them to a base board at the stated spans; print the panels hollow in PLA with 1.5 mm walls (about 52 g) and glue steel shot at each one's centre to reach its mass, so the centre of mass stays in the middle; cut the mat from 2 mm rubber sheet and the plate from 3 mm acetal sheet and tape both down. Stand the red and grey panels first, then lean the inner blue panel on the red one and the outer blue panel on the inner blue one.
scoring: Fall record: from the start of the trial, at every control step (20 Hz) in simulation and from the trial video on real arms, a panel whose 100 mm axis tilts more than 10 degrees from vertical, free or held, sets the score to 0 for the whole trial, and nothing later in the trial clears it, not even rebuilding the rack. The settled lean is 0.3 to 0.6 degrees, and every wrong order crosses the gate: lift the red panel while the inner blue panel leans on it, or the inner blue panel while the outer one leans on it, and the unsupported panel passes 10 degrees about 0.1 s later and swings into its slot to about 30 degrees, where its foot reaches the table. So the blue side comes out in one order, outer blue, inner blue, then red; the grey panel stands on its own and never needs to move. End state, judged when nothing moves (speed under 10 mm/s, spin under 0.5 rad/s), from a top photo, a tape measure and a phone level. A blue panel is parked when it stands with its long axis within 5 degrees of vertical, either end down, its lowest corner within 3 mm of the mat top (2 mm up) and all four corners of its base inside the mat's 80 x 240 mm outline. The red panel is inspected when it stands the same way on the plate, its lowest corner within 3 mm of the plate top (3 mm up) and its whole base inside the plate's 100 x 100 mm outline. The grey panel stands in place when it stands within 5 degrees of vertical with its centre within 10 mm of where it started. It stayed when, besides, it was never, at any control step, more than 10 mm from there along the table, tilted more than 5 degrees or lifted more than 3 mm off its rail; this is kept in the same record as falls, so setting it back does not restore its 0.2. Score with no fall: 0.2 for each parked blue panel; 0.4 more if the red panel is inspected while both blue panels are parked and the grey panel either stands in place or is parked; 0.2 more if, with all that, the grey panel stayed: 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8 or 1.0. Unloading from the outside in, grey panel included, scores 0.8, and so does moving the grey panel and setting it back. Success, which ends the trial, is 1.0 held for 1 s. Start state: nothing parked or inspected, 0. A panel lying, leaning more than 5 degrees, standing on another panel, on the rails, on the table, beside the mat or plate, still moving or held above its place earns nothing. The red panel earns nothing on the mat, nor on the plate while a blue panel is anywhere but the mat (blue panels nudged along their rails until they stand alone included), nor while the grey panel is anywhere but its rail or the mat. Panel yaw does not matter. In simulation, tilt, base corners and lowest corner come from each panel's centre and quaternion. The record is kept on every control step and cleared only when the simulator resets for a new trial; putting a panel back where it started, however exactly, does not clear it. Release: in simulation both grippers are read every control step, and while either gripper's pads are within 30 mm of any loose part the score is 0 and success cannot start, so a part held in a scoring place earns nothing; success needs the parts at rest and both grippers clear for 1 s. On real arms the photo after the arms park decides. The rack, mat and plate are fixed in simulation; on the real rig a trial in which one of them moves more than 5 mm scores 0.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Stand the red and grey panels centred on their rails, then the inner blue panel on its rail with its inner face against the red one and the outer blue panel on its rail with its inner face against the inner blue one, and let both lean; the outer blue panel's outer face is flush with its rail's outer edge and the inner blue panel's is 6 mm past its rail. The rack, mat and plate do not move. Run with -E object_jitter=0: the leaning start and the open-loop demo depend on it. In simulation only the simulator's reset, at the start of each trial, clears the fall and grey-panel record.
fidelity: Approximate: the panels are rigid 50 mm blocks standing in for thinner, flexible sheets, and they lean at 0.3 to 0.6 degrees rather than the few degrees of a real A-frame rack, so a fall here starts from almost upright. Rails, mat and plate are fixed colliders. One shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), matte colours, Earth gravity on a bench. A fall is scored, not simulated as damage.
